segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's nearly 2:00 in the afternoon when we reach Jennifer's family's apartment, and she's just gotten up. She's still eating a very late breakfast.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I'll finish my noodles, then I'll start packing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm with my co-worker, Emanuele Berry, and we're in a quiet working-class neighborhood in the part of Hong Kong that's called New Territories. It's a Sunday, so Jennifer is getting ready to do what she does every weekend-- what she did yesterday, in fact. That's why she slept late. She's going to a protest-- with a little backpack.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So this is the bag that I usually bring.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this is a maroon bag.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: It's a very small one. We have to keep everything light. So I always have a bottle of water and then many tissues. I have to bring a lot of tissues because we need to wipe our eyes when there is tear gas. And because I know how to do first aid, I always bring my first aid kit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The first aid kit is a little zip-up bag with roller bandages and gauze and gloves and stuff to sterilize a wound. Jennifer started at the volunteer ambulance corps in seventh grade and has used all this stuff at demonstrations. She packs her wallet and her AirPods.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Because I have to listen to songs.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Two batteries for her phone because she's on it constantly during protests, checking the continuously updated online maps that show where the police are and show escape routes. She packs a black T-shirt. The uniform of the Hong Kong protesters is black shirt, black pants, surgical masks to disguise their identities.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jennifer, by the way, is not her real name. But for the bus ride to the protest, she doesn't wear her uniform. She wears a striped maroon shirt.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, I wear a normal T-shirt when I go out so that no one can identify I am going to protest. And sometimes I bring makeup so that I can transform myself after the protest.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: I don't understand. How do you transform yourself? Like, what's the--

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I bring foundation-- very small, but can do everything.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How different are you going to work with that foundation?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: No, it looks like you're not going to protest. Because girls who are going to protest, they barely do makeup. But if girl is doing makeup, they're probably meeting someone. And so I bring this one. And then of course, I bring my brow pencil because it really can make you look like another person.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Eyebrows are very important, I agree.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah. [LAUGHS] And I bring lipstick. Sorry, it's a very small room.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So we're in your room. Your room has pink walls, and there is a bunk bed with the bed on the top and a desk underneath it.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, it's very typical Hong Kong girl's room.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For a Hong Kong protester to live at home with her mom and dad, that is not unusual in any way. If you know anything about the demonstrations that have overtaken Hong Kong since June, you know it's mostly young people in the city where rents are high. Jennifer is 22 and just graduated college. She's working her first entry-level job at a public relations firm.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I came to Hong Kong because there were things about the protests that I really did not understand, and we'll get to that. But one of the things that fascinated me once I arrived was learning what a routine the protests have become and what that was like for the people in them. This was mid-September, the 13th week of protests for Jennifer.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I'm not really worried because it's just like another day. I think I will meet up with two friends of mine. But I'm not sure if I am going to because they are couples so I don't want to be-- [LAUGHS] they are couple, so I don't want to be-- they always kiss next to me. So, mm, yeah.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Speak of the devil, it's her friend, the one who kisses your boyfriend at demonstrations. And she's calling with bad news. She was going to bring gas masks to the rally today. They'd order them from Amazon, Jennifer thinks. But now she's learned that bringing gas masks would be a bad idea. Because at the subway station--

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Police are searching everybody, including men, little ones, and young people like us. They're sharing their bags. And if they have any equipment with them like the gas mask, eye mask, whatever, they just arrest them, yeah. So my friend just asked me if it is a must for me to get the gas mask, so I told her that no, it is not a must. I don't want to risk my friend getting searched. So she told the other friend not to come out with equipment.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Not ideal, but she's gone without gas masks before. Jennifer grabs her knapsack, says bye to her mom, who tells her to come home early, a request that will be totally ignored. And we head outside. But then she turns and runs back.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What did you forget?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Umbrella. It is very important to have umbrella.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Even if it's not going to rain?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, it is not for the rain. It is for tear gas and bullets.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Rubber bullets, that is.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It works on bullets?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yes. Frankly, yes. No, no, I don't understand why, but always, those bullets, they slip off along the umbrella edge. So they just-- they don't get through the umbrella.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, protesters hide behind a wall of umbrellas when they're painting graffiti or dismantling a closed-circuit TV camera on the street, doing anything else they don't want the police to see.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As she and I and Emanuele head to the bus stop, we notice other young people carrying full-sized umbrellas on this totally sunny day.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Walking over here to the bus, are you looking around to see if-- other people you think are going to protest?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, you always want to know how many people are around you, right? Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, and so there's some young people on our left, two people standing next to you.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I think the girl probably is not because she brings a very small bag. But the tall guy, the tall guy in white shirt.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, and then the couple behind you, probably.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's like, are you on my side? Are you one of us? Once you're at the protest, everybody's in a mass so you don't really know who's on your team. Here in the neighborhood, it's kind of exciting to wonder who your allies might be.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The protests in Hong Kong have been international news for months, kicked off by people's fears that mainland China is threatening some very basic things about their city and their lives. But for all the coverage, here at our show, we felt like we weren't seeing many stories where we got to know anybody very well-- who they were, what exactly they expected was going to come out of the protests, given China's intransigence.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Three of us arrived in Hong Kong in mid-September, me and Emanuele and a co-worker, Diane Wu. I have to say, one of the things that was fascinating, given the ugly state of democracy here in the United States lately, was to be among so many young people who believe so intensely in democratic ideals and yearn so deeply for the basics, like normal elections and free speech and free assembly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Though, just in the last few weeks since we got to Hong Kong, we've watched the situation change dramatically. It's gotten much more violent, harsh new measures by the government.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This hour, we have the story of the change that we witnessed and what we think it might mean. If you haven't been following this story at all-- maybe you've been sitting this one out-- we're going to catch you up on what you need to know. We have all sorts of people from all sides of this that we want you to meet. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. This week, overseas with a lot of people who have some very American values. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, The Cursed Generation. OK, so what politicized thousands and thousands of people this much, that they've dropped their normal lives, and they're coming out every single weekend to protest? It's now been 18 straight weeks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Take Jennifer, for instance. She's somebody who worked at Abercrombie and Fitch during college. She told me on the bus to protest that's why her English is so good. She's somebody who wanted to be a singer. Actually got a chance to go pro when she was 16, but her mom quashed that, saying it was too much of a long shot and she should get an education and get a normal job. Jennifer was actually very surprised when I informed her that an American parent might have said the same exact thing.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Oh, I thought American dreams can be true, something like that, because I watched Glee.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So how did this Glee-watching, internet-savvy college grad in her first office job, how did she end up protesting in the street every weekend with tens or-- I don't know-- maybe it's hundreds of thousands of her peers? Well, for starters, Jennifer's 22, which means she's part of a special generation in Hong Kong.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I'm born in Hong Kong in 1997, right before the handover.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And here's a protester we're calling Alice.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: And I'm born in 1997.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Here's her friend we're calling Tiffany.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: I'm also born in 1997.

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: You can call me Yuen, and I'm born in 1997.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: So 1997 is the year when Hong Kong was handed over back to China from the British.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, let's just pause on these 22-year-olds for a minute for some quick history. As you may or may not know, Hong Kong sits on the edge of mainland China, right? It was a British colony for a really long time, starting in the 19th century. And then finally, in 1997, the British got out. They handed it over to China. And the idea was, there's going to be a 50-year transition period. After 50 years, China would fully be in charge. But during that 50 years, Hong Kong would be a democracy.

segments.speaker: Chris Patten
segments.text: Now, Hong Kong people are to run Hong Kong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's the last British governor of Hong Kong during the handover ceremony in 1997.

segments.speaker: Chris Patten
segments.text: That is the promise, and that is the unshakeable destiny.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But to be clear, Hong Kong had not been a democracy under Britain. But they were going to transition towards it over a bunch of years. And the hope was, after 50 years, in 2047, the Chinese government would let them stay a democracy-- which, at the time, did not seem like a crazy idea.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: China was opening up in all kinds of ways, though it wasn't clear how this was going to play out. And at the end of the day, after 50 years, in the year 2047, China was going to be able to do whatever it wanted in Hong Kong. These are the children born the year that clock started ticking.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And have you heard of the phrase "cursed generation?"

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: Yes, it was a joke among the 1997 people.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: It was pretty much a joke, pretty much a funny thing to us, because--

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: I think when we first joke about it, it's really primary schools, but--

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: The cursed generation is just what we've been joking around for all those years.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Originally, the joke had to do with a coincidence. They were cursed because of some weird, bad luck during some big childhood milestones they all went through together, like the year of their kindergarten graduation, the SARS virus hit Hong Kong. And the city shut down, graduations were canceled.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Six years later, when they should've had their elementary school graduation, same thing happened again, but with swine flu. And Jennifer remembers that her friends joked that when they graduated high school, it was going to be Ebola. And that's when they started using the word "cursed."

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I think that was around the time that JK Rowling wrote Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. Yeah, so many of us-- oh, we're the cursed child. Or we say that we are the chosen one because Harry Potter was the chosen one. All of us love Harry Potter.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So we always think that, oh, we are the chosen one. We have to face something special in our life. Or we are the cursed one. We have to face something bad or face something significant.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jennifer says the "chosen one" side of things didn't really kick in until their senior year of high school. It was 2014. They were 17, the 17th year since the handover. And that year, people in Hong Kong were still expecting that mainland China was going to let them start holding full-on elections, where they could choose their own leaders, as promised back in 1997. And that year, China announced it wasn't going to happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This led to a movement called the Umbrella Movement, headed by young people, teenagers, who'd learned their politics in these public school classes that all these 22-year-olds talk about as being instrumental in their thinking, classes that began as part of the handover called Liberal Studies classes that explained, among other things, the promises of 1997 and the rights of Hong Kong citizens.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They took to the streets, most of them for the first time, demanding to vote, carrying umbrellas, thousands of people in a vast procession down the streets in a protest movement that was almost entirely peaceful. And they lost. They didn't get the vote. After three months, the protests ended.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alice works for a multinational company in an entry-level job out of college. She's a management trainee. She says she went to some protests back then out of solidarity with her peers.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: I was just amazed by the other students.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But she did really get all the politics. That changed this June, when Hong Kong introduced the bill that would allow mainland China to extradite people from Hong Kong to be tried and punished in China under Chinese law. This was seen as a new and very menacing encroachment on the rights of Hong Kong citizens.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Since 1997, they'd been ruled by Hong Kong laws and Hong Kong courts, where everybody is presumed innocent with the rights we know in most democratic countries. Now, anybody could get thrown into the prisons and courts of communist China.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: I would say that that was the time when I first feel awakened, when I'm truly understanding what's happening when I first go to the march of the no extradition bill. And I was very, very emotional at that time because there is only around 7 million people in Hong Kong. But 1 million walk on the street with the same demand, with the same wish of having Hong Kong to remain its current state.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wanting Hong Kong to stay like it is with its own laws, separate from China. A week later, 2 million people came out.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: At the time, I was feeling very, oh my god, this is so touching. Why is people so united? And then the next second, the government just declares that, oh, we heard your voice, but we will be continuing on the bill on Tuesday. So that was a really big contrast.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: And in the morning, you see how peaceful things were. But at night, you see the police coming out and start brutally hitting people. It was really unforgettable to me because that was the first time when I witnessed with my real eyes that the police is chasing people. They are chasing students who did not do anything and start to beat them and arrest them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Other 22-year-olds also told us how radicalizing it's been to see police teargassing and beating peaceful protesters. And at this point-- I didn't understand this before we got to Hong Kong-- a lot of the emotion driving the protests is just about the police.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: Because the government is supporting them to do such things, and there is no penalty for them, even if they are doing things that are completely unacceptable to everyone.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Of course, nobody knows where this is going to lead by 2047, when China fully takes over Hong Kong. But for Jennifer and lots of other people her age, things are starting to feel pretty ominous. Was Hong Kong going to become just like any other Chinese city run by the communists?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When you're 50, what do you picture life here will be like?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I can picture that I will be super depressed because I super like comment on political things. I really cannot imagine the day that I cannot speak freely on internet, that we do not have that freedom of speech anymore. And I cannot imagine that there will come a day me and my friends commenting on the government would become a crime.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And you think that would happen.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yes, I do, when all the things that is happening in mainland China now, especially, I would say, in-- where is it-- Xinjiang.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Xinjiang.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, what is happening in Xinjiang will happen in Hong Kong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She's talking about internment camps where the Chinese are holding perhaps a million Uighurs and others.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: They say is re-education, but it's basically a concentration camp. They put people who do not agree with the government into the concentration camp and educate them. And they got monitored wherever and whenever they go. Everywhere is police. Police monitors everybody's move. And I do think that if we do not fight for our future, there will come a day Hong Kong will become like Xinjiang.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because she's politically active, this does not feel like an abstract threat. When these 22-year-olds picture who China's going to crack down on, it's them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tiffany's also in her first job out of college. She works at a bank. She asked us to replace her voice with an actress.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: Who knows whatever they would do to us? And under the extradition bill, who knows where we will go, what time we will disappear? That's what we fear of.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tiffany's heard of the social credit system that China has started to monitor and rate its citizens. She fears that if China decides that you're anti-government, it will make it impossible for you to get the job you want or rise in society. And the devices the China uses to monitor its population, an estimated 200 million surveillance cameras around the country with facial recognition software, they've been going up around Hong Kong, tens of thousands of them.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: Many, like me, are scared of being monitored and rated so that we will never, ever be free to do anything that we want under the monitoring of the Chinese government.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is something else I didn't understand before I came to Hong Kong. The protesters like Tiffany and Jennifer don't just fear what's going to happen to them in the future, with extradition laws or losing the internet or losing free speech. In their daily lives right now, they believe they're watching China already transforming Hong Kong, making it less like the Hong Kong they know and more like the mainland.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jennifer points to changes in the public school curricula. Like, she says, her seven-year-old nephew is speaking Mandarin in school five days a week. That didn't happen when she was a kid. Mandarin's what they speak in mainland China. In Hong Kong, people mostly speak in Cantonese and in English.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So all the Chinese classes are conducted in Mandarin. So he speaks Mandarin everyday, basically. He speaks Mandarin better than English.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Can you explain a little bit why Cantonese is so important?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Cantonese is more like an identity to us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's part of what makes Hong Kong Hong Kong. These days, when Jennifer pictures what her life is going to be like between now and 2047, she imagines her own kids going to public schools, not studying Cantonese, coming home and parroting the pro-government line that'll be the curriculum by then.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So, I do love kids. I really want to have kids. I want to have a football team of kids, really. But I just cannot imagine the life they will be having in Hong Kong later on. I cannot promise my kid a happy life if I am not certain about what will Hong Kong become.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You don't think there are children who are raised to be happy in mainland China?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Not the kind of happy that I think. Mainland China people, they think that they are happy because they can still live. But we want things more than just surviving in this society. We look for rights and freedoms and human rights. But the mainland China, they ignore all those things. They just think having a stable life, having kids, having food, a good place to live in is already happy enough. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Another change she says she's seeing right now in Hong Kong, she's upset at all the mainlanders moving there in her neighborhood, and university students that she and her friends encountered at college. So many mainlanders, she says.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I just feel really weird because I am born and raised in Hong Kong. I go to a local school, but then I have to be surrounded by all the mainlanders.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Does it bother you to be surrounded by mainlanders?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yes, actually, quite. But then we have 150 new immigrants from China to Hong Kong every day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, yeah, I'm just going to pause the tape there for a second. The total, by the way, is over a million mainlanders since 1997, roughly 45,000 a year. But I'm stopping the tape because I don't know how you're feeling about Jennifer, but this was a point we came to in a few interviews with these 22-year-olds. When you got them under the subject of mainlanders, get ready for a wave of totally bigoted opinions.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So especially I live in New Territories. So all the people surrounding you, you hear Mandarin, and then you start to see those less educated people, they're squatting next to the streets. I did witness a mainland lady having her children pee at the road. And I always hear mainland people yelling, shouting out for nothing in the mall. And always, they jump into the line-- everything. It bothers me a lot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Squatting, what do you mean squatting?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I don't know. They just squat on the roadside, waiting people.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They just sit and squat and wait.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, for nothing. They can squat for an hour.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: People in Hong Kong don't do that.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, we don't, 'cause who would squat at the road? Why can't you can't stand? Or why you can't just sit?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They're more comfortable.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: It just doesn't look good. It doesn't look good. It doesn't look civilized.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So for all the alarm that Jennifer and the cursed generation feel about the future, the parents are often not as alarmed about China taking more control of Hong Kong and about what the island's going to be like in 2047. Like Tiffany's parents, they hate her going out to protest every weekend.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: I think for my parents, they-- we really had some very serious fights.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And they think, we'll just let China take over Hong Kong. It'll be fine.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: I think my parents, some of the older generation just don't believe, or they are not brave enough to open up their eyes and see what is actually going to happen. They just feel like they did not do anything wrong. As long as you did not do anything wrong, then you'd be fine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's galling about this for Tiffany is that she feels like she's being the responsible one, fighting for everybody's future. And they're telling her not to protest. She was like, maybe if your parents had done this themselves years ago, things wouldn't be so bad today.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: I'm 22 years old. And in the past, when I was younger, they have never stood up like us or fight like us to ask for what they are promised in 1997.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's funny. When you talk about it, you're mad at your parents about it.

segments.speaker: Tiffany
segments.text: I just feel like-- I mean, I don't understand why they would not want these rights or why they don't think that something bad is going to happen in the next 50 years.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Tiffany and Jennifer and so many others, they've kind of given over their lives to protesting. They work during the week, protest on the weekends. They say they don't have much time in their lives for much else. But what's interesting is, they don't think it's going to work. Most of our interviewees told us that. They don't think China is going to give in. Again, here's Jennifer.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I am pretty much pessimistic, actually. I do wish that one day, we all succeed. We want a democratic Hong Kong, but now, I just don't see a way out. It's been three months. We've been trying each and every step. We've broke into the legislative council. We have more than 1,000 people got arrested. But the government is still trying to ignore all of this.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: If you feel so pessimistic about the results, why still go? Why are you still going out every weekend?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: At least the governments see that we are not that-- how do we say-- we are not that obedient. So we have to continuously tell the government that we are not satisfied with what they are giving us. So we have to do it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Again, here's Alice.

segments.speaker: Alice
segments.text: I think even if we have to lose, we need to leave our true thoughts in history. We need to let the people behind us know that we've tried.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: 2047 is coming, and this is a very grand thing to say, but so many of these curse generation kids feel like they have a special destiny. Alex preferred to speak to us through an interpreter. She's a frontline protester, builds barricades, has been arrested.

segments.speaker: Alex
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: I think we're actually lucky because we grew up with people who thought the same way. And we realized that when we turn 50, it's the end of our freedoms. I'm 22 now, and I imagine that when I'm 25, that's really halfway until the bomb explodes.

segments.speaker: Interpreter
segments.text: And so if we don't do anything, by the time we're 50 years old, it would be awful. I don't want our children to have the same battle. And then when we're 50, we'll look back and think that we didn't do enough. Our birthday is like a countdown to the end. And so, more so than other people, I feel like my generation, we have a duty to do more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Again, here's Jennifer.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: If we were born earlier, probably I would become my dad and mom. And if I were born later, I would probably become those little kids speaking Mandarin better than Cantonese. So I am happy that I am born in 1997. We are in the middle. We have the chance to know what is freedom, and we are experiencing that our freedom is being taken away. And that's why we are the group who step up first to fight for it.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: I think we're getting off here. I think we are getting off.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After an hour bus ride, we get to the protest. This is Act Two, The Fight. Once you're off of the bus, Jennifer ducks into a public restroom and comes out in black shirt, black pants, black mask over her face, hair pulled back in a ponytail. And we head on to a street where we're surrounded by hundreds of people dressed exactly like her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A big shopping district, the stores closed, and no cars. All the side streets have been blocked off with barricades by the protesters-- scaffolding and fencing, trashcans, and orange construction cones piled in the street. They do an efficient job. We meet up with Jennifer's friends by a big Victoria's Secret store.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: My friend.

segments.speaker: Female Friend
segments.text: Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nice to meet you, Ira.

segments.speaker: Male Friend
segments.text: Nice to meet you, man. Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Very nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: The couple who always kiss in front of me.

segments.speaker: Female Friend
segments.text: What? I'm not.

segments.speaker: Male Friend
segments.text: No, we didn't. We didn't.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For the record, I'm with them all afternoon-- no kissing at all. The city is giving permission for fewer protests these days, and this is an unsanctioned demonstration we're at, which means that everybody here is breaking the law. Anyone is subject to arrest, which affects crowd size. The maximum penalty is five years-- 10 years, if you're convicted of rioting-- which is why all the protesters are so scared of getting arrested all the time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But despite that, the beginning of the protest has the feeling of a block party. People strolling, chatting-- you see a few parents and kids. Some non-protesters cut through the crowd, running errands. But an hour into all this, I look around and realize-- no families, no kids. It's not feeling like a block party at all. People are standing on top of fences, trying to see what's ahead of us. They're starting to put on gas masks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Describe what you're seeing.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: The protesters in the Thomas Street are moving backwards, so we assume that there are riot police on the other end of the road. There is tear gas fired over there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's like two or three blocks away. We walk towards the police and the tear gas, past teams of protesters who are knocking bricks out of the sidewalk with long steel tools.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the idea is what?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: To put on the road so, later on, the riot police cannot run that fast.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, people throw bricks at the police. We march straight to the frontlines, where hundreds of protesters are massed on a side street. The police are just half a block away, but we can't really see them through the crowd. And then a whole wave of tear gas canisters arcs towards us, hits us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And lots of people, us included, run back a ways, half a block away. Jennifer calmly administers saline solution into strangers' eyes. The controls on my recorder got knocked around running through the smoke, so I do not have a decent recording of that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is the role that she's assigned herself in the protest-- first aid, helping anybody who requires it. She even brought energy candy specifically to give out to people whose energy is flagging. After being driven back, Jennifer and her two friends and I wait for the smoke to clear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this happens at every protest?

segments.speaker: Male Friend
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Basically.

segments.speaker: Male Friend
segments.text: Basically.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what do we do now?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: We tidy up ourselves and go again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And when you get to the police, what are you going to do?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: We're going to stand in front of them. If we have a chance, we're going to fight them back. Our goal is to make them to retreat their front line.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: After a couple minutes, we head back toward the front line.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, we're walking forward to its corner, where it's this blue-- [COUGHS]

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: And then we wait around. A water cannon goes off, blasting water that is dyed blue, laced with stuff that stings your skin. More tear gas, and we pull back a little. Then we move forward, wait again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is both suspenseful and boring.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Sometimes there's not always a purpose. Sometimes we sitting at the back is just as a support. We just act as a support to those at the front.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Support like, if something happens, you'll do first aid?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Something like this, but also they know that there are many people behind them. It is important to give them some mental support as well. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So many protesters are like Jennifer. They feel like it's their job to support the people at the front, who are the hardcore ones, who push back against police and throw Molotov cocktails, and chase police with sticks and metal rods, and tear stuff down to build barriers to slow the police, wearing full gear, helmets and goggles and gas masks and gloves.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Finally, the frontliners yell that they want room to retreat. And so we need to retreat. And so we fall way back, a couple blocks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So now we're just standing here.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, because we always support. Our assistance is like a support to those in the front line.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But I don't understand. So the police want us out of there. They push, they fire tear gas. They spray blue water on everybody. We move back. And then we stand here, and what's our goal?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: This has been a very frequently asked question. Nowadays, we're just trying to stand on our own ground, not to be dispersed that easily.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's it. Just, the goal is to just stay out as long as you can.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then eventually, the police will push you off the street? So in other words, it's exactly like the entire protest movement leading to 2047. Just try to slow them down as much as you can.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the end, China will win. But for as long as you can, you'll just stand here in the street.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: It is pretty sad to say so, but I guess that's pretty much accurate. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What are they yelling?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: They ask people to start moving.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then we headed to a massive retreat, as the police advance towards us. And for the first time, there seems to be actual real fear. We're running down the streets and side roads. We get separated from Jennifer's friends and from Emanuele, dodging the police, and finally, taking refuge in a church. There are safe houses like this around Hong Kong that protesters duck into. It takes over an hour, and finally, the coast is clear.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Jennifer calls her friend to pick her up. They're volunteer drivers for the protesters, part of the infrastructure they've created. Jennifer changes out of her black T-shirt into civilian clothes. No makeup-- she's too tired, she says, and no need, if she's getting picked up.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she heads home.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Say goodbye to Emanuele for me as well. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As her car pulled away, across the street on Queens Road, there was an endless row of police vehicles headed in the other direction, just dozens of them, blue and red lights flashing. And as night went on, things became violent. A woman approached us on the sidewalk, upset about police beating somebody, and showed us video that she'd shot of it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the protesters were violent as well. The newspapers had accounts of six of them beating up a middle-aged man, kicking and shouting at him. They set fire to a subway station. They do that a lot because lots of protesters think Hong Kong subway-- the MTR-- colludes with the police. That's why Jennifer prefers the bus, even though it's less convenient.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Every protester we interviewed supports the violence. They support it because they feel like they have no other options, that it's the only way they can get the government to respond to them. A few told us, back in June, they marched peacefully against the extradition bill and got nothing. Then they got violent, and the bill was withdrawn. It worked.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And violence has become a way to defend themselves. Setting fires and building barricades slows police, who were coming after them. So they support the violence, or they at least understand it. Emanuele talked to them about that. We're at Act Three of our show, On Civil Disobedience. Here's Emanuele.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: When I started asking protesters about violence, a couple of them said, we're not violent like Americans. Our tolerance for it is much lower. So getting to this point to being OK with violence isn't something we did lightly. And a lot of them explained to me that they didn't always think radical tactics were OK.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: What changed their opinion was the way police responded to peaceful protest. That being shot at with water cannons, tear gassed, seeing someone knocked unconscious, beaten with batons, handcuffed and kicked, groups of thugs beating and attacking people with hammers, clubs, and knives, watching all this and being subjected to it-- that's what got a lot of people on board with violence. Now some protesters throw Molotov cocktails, vandalize buildings, and chase police with sticks and rods. Ira and I talked with one protester, Yuen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you think it would be acceptable for the protesters to kill police?

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: I hope they do so.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You do?

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: I do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: If police died, what do you think would happen next?

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: We would die, too. Protesters will die, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And if things get that violent between the protesters and the police and protesters are being killed, do you think Hong Kong will get democracy?

segments.speaker: Yuen
segments.text: I can't tell at the moment.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: So many people we talked with expected someone to die-- a protester or a police officer. Most thought it would help the movement put pressure on the government. This hasn't happened yet, but destruction and violence are giving way to bizarre scenes throughout the city. My co-worker Diane and I went to this protest at a mall, one of many in Hong Kong.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Sometimes the entire city can feel like one giant Chinese shopping mall connected by subway. The stores are all open. The mall is full of people. But not many people are shopping. The entire premise of this protest is to go to the mall and not shop.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The mall is five stories. Each tier has railings that look out over a central atrium. There are families, kids, older folks. Some people are in black. Others are just in their regular day clothes. They chant. They sing the protester anthem, "Glory to Hong Kong," over and over.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: [PROTESTERS SINGING]

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: At one point, someone starts handing out paper, and suddenly hundreds of people are folding paper cranes. Then, an act of gentle vandalism. There's this machine that prints out reservation receipts for the restaurant called Jade Garden. The protesters hijack it, forcing it to spit out hundreds of receipts. They tape the receipts together and string them from one end of the atrium to the other and back again a few times.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: They target Jade Garden because one of the company's founders has a daughter who supports Beijing. That's how far things have gone in Hong Kong. Businesses are labeled either yellow or blue-- yellow for the ones that support the protesters, blue for the police and government. There's even a Google Map that tells you if a business is one or the other.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Soon, things in the mall start to shift. Diane and I watch a group of about a dozen protesters enter a pro-China bakery, owned by the same company that owns Jade Garden. They start taunting the staff.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: There's umbrellas up.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: They're blocking so you can't really see inside of it.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Is the person who works in there still in there?

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yeah-- well, she was a minute ago.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: OK, something fell.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: They knocked over a display.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Before things can escalate any further, the workers force the protesters out, close the store gates, and barricade themselves in. A restless energy takes over. It's like the protesters are looking for something to confront, something to disturb. But the thing they're fighting against is the existential threat of China. And that's not really in the mall.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They march to more pro-China businesses in the mall. The alarm starts going off, and a PA announcement says, "The mall is very crowded. Please be careful." Then word comes police are on their way, and some mood that feels like a mix of fear and adrenaline fills the space.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Protesters begin to build barriers out of whatever is not nailed to the ground, blocking doorways, creating obstacles. They want to stop the police from entering from the subway entrance of the mall. They start throwing trash cans down the escalators. A group rips a six-foot TV screen out of a wall to use as part of a blockade.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The PA announcement remains the same. "Please be careful. The mall is very crowded." They open an emergency firehose. Someone brings giant jugs of oil, which they add to the water. The tile floor of the mall lobby is now a little lake that police will have to cross. A woman slips and falls.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And while all this destruction is happening, the shoppers, the older folks, even a few families, they don't leave. They're on the upper levels of the mall, looking over the railing, like they're watching a sporting event or something. I'm super uncomfortable. The protester next to us, Chan, is so chill.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Have you been to a protest like this before?

segments.speaker: Chan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Does this feel normal?

segments.speaker: Chan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Is that weird that it's normal, though?

segments.speaker: Chan
segments.text: Yes, but it's been 100 days, so.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: The police eventually come, but they meet the protesters outside the mall. They throw tear gas. Protesters threw a Molotov cocktail. Smoke and gas waft through Snoopy World, a mini theme park on one of the mall's upper levels. Giant statues of Linus and Peppermint Patty, along with dozens of shoppers and protesters, who lined the outdoor balconies, all watch the confrontation between police and protesters unfold below.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: There's this thing that protesters say to each other-- never sever ties. Sometimes they even say, never sever ties even if there's a nuclear explosion. Basically, if another protester does something you disagree with-- say, set something on fire, beat someone up-- you don't criticize them or cut them off.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: My co-worker Diane saw an extreme example of this at a protest about a week later. It was a very peaceful protest in a park at night. So serene, Diane said she felt she could only whisper. Then a guy starts waving a big Chinese flag around. Protesters start shouting at him. He rips a poster out of one girl's hands. That's when the mob rushes in.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Oh, shoot. There's someone who's on the ground. And then their head's getting smashed, and they're kicking them.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Dozens of people walk by. And if anyone has a problem with this, they don't show it. He's left face down on the ground, bleeding from his head. Eventually, someone gets a first aid person to help.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Emanuele Berry is one of the producers of our show. She used to live next door to Hong Kong in Macau for about a year. Coming up, you're a protester. You think the police are utterly immoral and indefensible. So, what do you do about the cop who happens to be your dad? That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program, Umbrellas Up, stories from Hong Kong and what it's like for people to live through over 100 days of protests there. I traveled to Hong Kong with my co-workers, Diane Wu and Emanuele Berry. We have arrived at Act Four of our show. Act Four, Good Cop, Bad Cop.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So as an American visiting Hong Kong for the first time, one of the things that kind of killed me was hearing that before the last few years of protests, people were really into the police. They were trusted. They were respected. And it was only the last few years, especially the last few months of protests, that changed all that. At a rally, I actually saw people chanting at a row of cops that they hoped that they and their families would die.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And feelings about who to side with, the police or the protesters, they've gotten so intense, it's tearing families apart. On the Telegram app, there's a whole channel for protesters who get kicked out by their parents and need a place to live.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alan Yu grew up in Hong Kong. He knows a family that is very far apart on this. The son is a protester. The dad is a retired police officer. And Alan had them sit down and do what nobody in Hong Kong is doing-- talk to each other. There is really no dialogue between police and protesters anywhere in Hong Kong as far as we could tell. Here's Alan.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: I've known this family since I was six. I knew them because of my friend, Jonathan. I rode the school bus with him every day. His father, Peter, was the first policeman I knew in real life. I was excited to talk to him because you never hear what the police think about the protests. Police here are not really allowed to talk to the press.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Peter's retired, but still very connected to the force. So before the family all sat down together, I asked Peter to get together with me and my producer, Emanuele. I hadn't seen him since I was 12. Back then, people called me "Yu-don," which means fish ball, because the Cantonese for fish sounds like my surname, Yu, and because I was fat.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: I won't recognize you on the street. I won't. I won't.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Oh, yeah? Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Serious. I'm serious.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: OK. All right, I guess it's a compliment. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: He used to be very cute.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Yeah, how?

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: He used to be very fat.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: As a kid, I liked Peter. He'd take time off work to stop by during recess and buy us chips and other snacks. My friend Jonathan would have his birthday parties at the police station, which we loved-- big barbecues, other policemen around. Peter was the cool dad.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: People in Hong Kong trusted, even revered, the police back then. One of the most popular TV shows was a cop show, [CHINESE], where the police were heroes. Peter's hair is gray now. He's tall, athletic. He plays tennis.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: My nickname in tennis-- I don't know why. My nickname in tennis is Federer. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Federer.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Federer.

segments.speaker: Emanuele Berry
segments.text: Oh, are you good?

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Federer Roger. I don't know why. Maybe my skill. I don't know. I don't know why. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: He still likes his dad jokes. I cannot imagine Peter ever doing what I've been seeing in these videos-- beating up unarmed protesters, kicking people on the ground. I thought surely he would object to some of those things and that his views would be complicated.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: From what you've seen in recent months, has there been anything that the police have done that you think you would disagree with?

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Nothing is perfect. But as a whole, in general, I think the police are doing a pretty good job. If it is in other police force in other countries, just look at the casualties. Just look at the column of fatal numbers. It won't be zero.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: I ask him about different situations the police have been criticized for. I even show him videos of police brutally arresting people, things I think are clearly wrong. But he always seems to have a justification for the way police behave. He says you are judging the police based on what you see in these clips. That's not fair. You don't know what the officer was facing.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: The social media only show the part of police hitting people. But one minute ago, they've been attacked by lots of people. So one minute later, he react to the mob attacking them. So what you can see is one minute after, but you did not see the full picture.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: He's not conflicted about police, and he isn't very sympathetic to protesters. He thinks the protests are destroying Hong Kong. The extradition bill is OK. He doesn't think China will end free speech in Hong Kong, and protesters' fear of China is way overblown and naive.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Hong Kong being part of China. Come on. Wake up, people. Wake up. This is the fact. Whether China is good or bad, Hong Kong is part of China. If you don't like it, those people waving the United States flag, waving the Union Jack flag, if England takes you, you can go to England, yeah. You can go to Florida. Go to California. Yeah. Go. Go. If Trump takes you, yeah, go.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: I'd already been worried how this family conversation was going to go. Hearing what Peter believed did not help. Peter told me he understands that Jonathan goes to protests, but doesn't ask him about it because he doesn't want any details. Jonathan said he does not ask his dad what he thinks of the way police beat and tear gas protesters for the same reason.

segments.speaker: Jonathan
segments.text: It's just like if he says something-- if he says something that completely doesn't make sense to me, it sort of brings him down as a person. It's just like, I would feel like he's just, yeah, not who I thought he was, yeah.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: And it scares you to--

segments.speaker: Jonathan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: --think that could be true.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this family does not talk about the protests at all. Tennis, yes. Soccer, yes. Pets, great. But no politics-- till tonight. They've agreed to have the conversation they've been avoiding after dinner. Jonathan's mom, Alva, washes the dishes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [ALVA HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I recognize the song right away. I'm surprised she's humming it in front of Peter. It's the protesters' new anthem, "Glory to Hong Kong." Alva is on Jonathan's side. She works with lawyers, including some in the pro-democracy camp.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I ask if Peter knows what that song is. She says, maybe. That's kind of how it's been going between her and her husband. No real discussion, but the occasional passive aggressive comment while they're watching the news, or some passive aggressive humming during dishes. This is another reason Jonathan avoids bringing up the protests. He doesn't want to start a fight between his parents.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: What would the worst scenario be like?

segments.speaker: Jonathan
segments.text: Someone moving out, I guess. Yeah, because they can't stand it anymore. Yeah, I guess living apart would be the worst case scenario, I believe. Because that sort of officially means that you're no longer together, sort of, yeah.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: That could be his mom, or his dad, or him.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: We all sit at the dinner table. I don't know why they agreed to talk about this. Maybe just because I've known them for so long, and I asked. Or I hope maybe part of them wanted to talk, and I was just a good excuse. Peter's facing me, and Jonathan and Alva are next to me. Jonathan has their dog, Loki, named after the Marvel character, on his lap.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: The conversation starts with all of them saying, in different ways, it's fine that we don't talk about this. We all have mutual respect. Instead of talking to each other or looking at each other, they're talking to me or looking at the dog. It feels all very careful, proper, and calm. This continues for half an hour. Then, everything changes when Peter uses the word "compromise."

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Compromise-- it's basically the government line. That's what Hong Kong's chief executive Carrie Lam says, that the protesters should stop protesting. And after that, the two sides can talk. Alva and Jonathan hear that as meaning the protesters should back down. They both lay into Peter.

segments.speaker: Jonathan
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alva
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Alva says the police are the ones who need to change. They have to calm the situation. Peter says the police are doing their job. I don't know why, when the police arrest people for fighting or breaking stuff, it's treated as weird. It's illegal, so arrest them. No problem.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Jonathan says, OK, yes, arrest them. But how much force does the police need to use? Sometimes a person just asks the police a question, and they still get arrested or beaten. Or people who are already on the ground, kneeling, subdued, they still get beaten. Peter doesn't respond. Then they argue, openly argue for the first time, about one of the protesters' main demands, something the government refused to budge on-- to start an independent investigation into police behavior.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Peter keeps repeating the same thing over and over, like he's been backed into a corner, that there's no need for an independent investigation. Now is not the right time.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: The city already has a system in place to investigate complaints about the police.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [SPEAKING CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: They talk a little longer, but it doesn't go anywhere. Alva tells me later she had other things she could have brought up, but decided against it. She didn't want her husband to feel trapped. The word she used was [CHINESE], which translates as, dead corner. No place to go.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: Preserving the family was more important to her than trying to win an argument. Later, Jonathan told me he still loves his dad, but he's given up hope that his father could be a reasonable human being, at least when it comes to the police.

segments.speaker: Alan Yu
segments.text: When I started this, I was kind of naive. I thought maybe Jonathan and his mother and father, people who actually want to understand each other, could talk about this in a productive manner. And that if they could, maybe there was hope that the rest of us could. But now, I don't have a lot of hope.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Alan Yu. He's normally a reporter for WHYY's show The Pulse.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Five, A Slow Boat to China. So what about all the people living in Hong Kong who have no problem with China, who like China? There's a lot of them, and they hold their own demonstrations, which are pretty small-- flag parties where flash mobs show up at malls and wave Chinese flags and sing the Chinese national anthem.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the big day to celebrate China normally would be October 1, National Day, the anniversary of the Communist Party founding the modern Chinese state. And this year was going to be a big one. It was the 70th anniversary.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the people who support mainland China were kind of resentful, because this day was supposed to be this huge holiday for them, but anticipating massive protests, the city shut down. Fireworks were canceled. Trains weren't running. Almost all the malls were going to be closed. The protesters had ruined the day again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So in defiance, the pro-China people organized an anthem singing party for the morning of the first. Our co-worker, Diane Wu, went.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: The party took place at 8:30 in the morning on a boat. Not just any boat-- on the Star Ferry, this iconic Hong Kong commuter sightseeing boat on the harbor. The ferries are these beautiful old boats from colonial times with names like Silver Star, Northern Star, Twinkling Star. And today, one of them is going to get completely covered with bright red Chinese flags.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A couple dozen people are gathering at the ferry terminal. They're mostly strangers, know each other loosely from previous flash mobs and get-togethers.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SHOUTING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: "I love China," they shout.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SHOUTING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: "Support the police."

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SHOUTING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: It's kind of funny when you think about it, all these people up so early on their day off, getting on a boat to sing the national anthem together. It's also a little dark, because there's a real threat of violence against people who don't support the protest.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: One of these flag parties two weeks ago at a mall devolved into a brawl when protesters showed up. People on both sides got beat up. And so going out on a ferry to shout pro-China slogans is strategic. Once you're on the boat out at sea, you ought to be safe from a counter-protest. As one guy put it--

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Well, we've been living in terror for the last three months because the people on the other side, the rioters, they're really good at the terrorizing tactics. They make you feel that you should be afraid of speaking up and speaking out against them because they're so organized.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: In the terminal, everyone gathers in a semicircle, holding special holiday issues of the China Daily and singing the Chinese national anthem together.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SINGING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: It's a little shaky. The guy leading it told me he just learned the words a couple of weeks ago. Most of the people here, best as I can tell, are not mainlanders who grew up with the anthem. The ones I talked to were all from Hong Kong. Being this into China is new for them, something that only happened when the protests got bad enough that they found themselves rallying around this new flag.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: And it's not always comfortable. I'm getting on the boat with Daniel, the guy who was griping about being terrorized, when someone puts a heart-shaped sticker on him.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: You just got a Chinese flag sticker stuck on you.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Yes, yeah. I feel a little cringey about this.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: I'm not exactly that red. Compared to a lot of people here, I'm not the most red person.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Red, in the crayon box of the Hong Kong protests, refers to being pro-China, versus blue for the government and yellow for the protesters. Daniel almost didn't come this morning, actually. It's not really his scene. He sees being this patriotic about China as kind of dorky. Moreover--

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: I always tell my friends I would never want to live in China, because there's a lot of things in China that I can't accept if I were to be forced to live in China.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: The two things he can't accept that we end up talking about are the lack of free speech and censored access to the internet.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: But the truth is, I live in Hong Kong and I get to retain my almost unchecked freedom for 28 more years. And it's such a sweetheart deal for Hong Kong people.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: I pointed out to him that after 28 years, it's very possible those freedoms would disappear. And he had the same response that I heard from other people who don't like the protests. He was like, well, sure, maybe.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: Well, I guess, you're talking me to appreciate the young people's perspectives. But in exchange for the freedom that they fight for, they're wreaking havoc, and they're destroying law and order.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: So in the balance, it's not worth it to you.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: If I were to choose between this, if China say, in order to have law and order, I will need to sacrifice the freedom the same way Chinese people have in Hong Kong, I would accept that balance. This is unacceptable, the whole unorganized chaos, revolution, and the havoc they wrought in Hong Kong. It's completely unacceptable. I will give up the freedom the way they do in China to stop this.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: It's a big jump from I could never live in China to I would sacrifice my freedom just to get this to stop. But the intensity of the protests and his frustration with what he is experiencing in the city have driven him to at least try on this extreme idea.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Daniel's 40, works in finance. He lived in the US for 12 years. He's a football fan. Roots for the Chicago Bears because he likes the tenacious defense. He says he wasn't politically involved before all this. Went to one of the big peaceful protests last spring, more to watch than to participate.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: But that changed one day when he was watching a livestream of the young protesters storming the legislative council. He was surprised how ferocious they seemed, how even the police officers looked a little scared.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: At that moment, I suddenly realized, oh, we're actually very close to a revolution. It could happen. It just never occurred to me that Hong Kong would go through that. It's both stunned and anxiety about unknown. Anxiety-- things can change abruptly. If there isn't a revolution, it's going to force the hand of the Chinese government to crack down on it violently.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: And anything can happen. I could lose all the privilege I have as a Hong Kong citizen-- protection of common law, freedom of speech, but also freedom of speech protected by common law. Nobody in China enjoy this freedom, but-- if it gets to a certain point, we can lose all of these privileges, which I treasure.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: He woke up the next morning to see that the coverage was wall-to-wall about police brutality. To Daniel, it seemed like everyone was leaving out the fact that the protesters had started it, which seemed deeply unjust to the police.

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: And that's when I started turning blue. When I felt that the police were smeared unfairly, I took my side. I chose to be on the police's side.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Other people sided against the protest for different reasons. A big one I heard was the disruption they caused. The security guard told me he had to transfer four times to get home by night because of subway shutdowns.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: A woman trying to get cash out of an ATM that had been destroyed by protesters said, if you're mad at the government, take it out on the government. You're only hurting people like me. A man said to me, sadly, Hong Kong is our home. Why are they destroying it?

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SINGING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: The crowd on the boat finishes belting out the national anthem a second time, when, suddenly, everyone rushes to the railing.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Everyone's waving at the sea police. They all ran to one side of the boat. It feels like it might tip over.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Everyone crammed together on one side in a position that's a little precarious. That's kind of like Daniel's world right now. He felt pushed to choose a team. Like it or not, these are his new people. He doesn't think like them, exactly. But he feels more aligned with these Chinese nationalists on this boat waving at the police than with the angry protesters ganging up on them, even if those protesters ultimately want the same thing he does-- to preserve their freedoms in Hong Kong.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [SINGING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sitting on the upper deck of the Star Ferry, this was actually the first time Daniel had ever sung the national anthem in public. He told me later, as he sang, he was surprised to find that he felt something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Diane Wu is the managing editor of our show, and she also has one more story for us. I'm going to set this up. It is Act Six of our show. Act Six, Two Weeks Later.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So October 1 wasn't just a big day for supporters of mainland China. If anything, I think it was even more anticipated by pro-democracy protesters. They knew China did not want to be embarrassed by demonstrations in Hong Kong on that day, such a big anniversary. And in the weeks leading up to it, several of them told us that they were worried. What kind of crackdown was going to come on October 1, or maybe in the days before it? Would the government try to shut them down?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And sure enough, the weekend before October 1, there were tons of police, undercover cops posing as protesters, surge in arrests. And on October 1, something happened that several of our interviewees predicted. For the first time, a protester was shot with a real bullet-- a teenager.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the days after that, things descended. The government banned wearing face masks in public, which caused a huge backlash in the streets. Another teenager, a 14-year-old, was shot by police. Both teenagers survived, by the way. A protester slashed an officer's neck with a box cutter. A bomb went off next to a police car.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jennifer, the protester that I went to the demonstration with in mid-September, she went to all those protests in the days before October 1, and then she was out on October 1, that big violent day. And Diane caught up with her the day after that, October 2, to see how she was doing, and to see what she made of it all.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: I met up with Jennifer at the MTR station in Tsuen Wan on a Wednesday. She'd taken the MTR only because she was in a big rush to meet me after work.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: You had a long day?

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, very long one. It is a really sad thing, after yesterday.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: She's talking about the protester who was shot. It actually happened just a short walk from where we're standing. The last few days of protests had been especially bad. Jennifer was in the middle of the crowd when dozens of special tactics police officers exploded out of a hidden door, sprinting after protesters and tackling them to the ground. People hadn't seen this before. It caused a wave of panic. Everyone fled in terror, including Jennifer.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Her phone was flooded with images of arrested protesters, pinned on the ground by riot police, face down with their wrists tied behind them. Later, she met her friend, the one who went to the protest with Ira and her, and found out that in the rush, she had gotten trapped. She came really close to getting arrested.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: All of a sudden, everything was so close to me. A very important friend of mine nearly getting arrested, and all the pictures and footages I could see after the day. Everything just was so-- was just too much for me.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Yeah, it was too close.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Jennifer's deeply fearful of getting arrested. Remember, it could mean years in prison. After all of that, on October 1, she was almost too scared to go protest, but braved it anyways. Then, police started to fire tear gas at people up ahead of them.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: We were on our way walking from Tsuen Wan to Kwai Fong. And I realized that I couldn't keep walking. I started to realize that I just feel different. Two weeks ago, when I was with Ira, I could still feel it is safe to run. I'm going to be fine. And I could still like run without any hesitation. But yesterday, I just feel like I was so terrified. I started to shake from the inside. And then I didn't know what to do.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: She panicked, started crying. Her boyfriend helped her get home.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: So I had to leave yesterday. But then, actually on my way home, there was a friend of mine. I think he was just joking and saying, you left your teammate behind. He sent this to me.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Yeah, so I was immediately crying. I cried out immediately and really could not control myself because I didn't want this. I don't want to leave my teammates behind. I don't want to leave anyone behind. But I don't want to be a burden. And then all of a sudden, yesterday, I couldn't do anything at all.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: The police strategy of clamping down on the protests by outlawing almost all of them, then flooding the streets with riot police and arresting tons of people, this is the toll it's taking. And of course, this is one way the whole thing could end. Maybe it'll scare people off.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: Oh, I saw my boyfriend.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Jennifer's boyfriend, Joe, shows up. He's got his shirt tucked in, a new protest tactic from this weekend. The idea is to try and expose undercover police who wouldn't be able to tuck their shirts in over their guns and batons. Joe's here for moral support because, incredibly, Jennifer is now on her way to another protest. We're headed to a soccer stadium across the street from where the protester was shot. Jennifer figures she'll stay as long as she can tolerate.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: We walk onto the field. It's a big solemn group of people in their work and school clothes, all facing the bleachers.

segments.speaker: Jennifer
segments.text: There are a lot of people. Not sure where they are looking at, but I think they are just waiting for a moment to mourn.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: It's a kind of vigil for the protester in the hospital. Jennifer and Joe put on black surgical masks.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: Everyone has their phones up with their lights on.

segments.speaker: Diane Wu
segments.text: [SINGING IN CHINESE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We go into the streets, Jennifer's on edge. Every time she hears a loud noise, she squeezes Joe's hand. She'll stay out until 10:30. Then she'll get dinner, go home, go to bed. In the morning, Jennifer will be at work again, at her job where she can't let her bosses know where she was the night before.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Overnight, the road cleaners will come out with backhoes to clear the barricades. They'll paint over the graffiti, fix the smashed street lights, tidy up the piles of bricks in the gutters, erasing their protests as they have so many days before, turning the city back to normal, except, of course, it can't be normal again.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Diane Wu.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our website, thisamericanlife.org. This American Life is delivered to public radio stations by PRX, the Public Radio Exchange. Thanks, as always, to our program's co-founder, Mr. Torey Malatia. You know, he'll never forget his first time on a carousel. The way he tells the story, he gets on a horse and starts to go around--

segments.speaker: Daniel
segments.text: At that moment, I suddenly realized, oh, we're actually very close to a revolution. It could happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
